rewritten_text:
‘Do you come back often?’

‘This is the first time I've been here since.’

‘Mine too.’

The moon began to rise, and I remembered that peaceful gaze toward the white ceiling, now gone forever. The moon began to rise, and I remembered the squeeze of my hand when I spoke the last words he ever heard.

Estella was the first to break the silence between us.

‘I've often hoped and planned to return, but one thing after another has prevented me. Poor, poor old place!’

The first moonbeams lit the silvery mist and caught the tears falling from her eyes. Unaware that I could see them, and trying to overcome them, she said softly:

‘As you were walking here, were you wondering how it came to be left like this?’

‘Yes, Estella.’

‘The land is mine. It's the only possession I haven't given up. Everything else has slipped away from me, little by little, but I've held on to this. Keeping it was the only thing I firmly resisted over, through all those miserable years.’

‘Will they build on it?’

‘At last, yes. I came to say goodbye before it changes. And you,’ she said, showing an interest in this wanderer that touched me, ‘you still live abroad?’

‘I do.’

‘And you're doing well, I'm sure?’

‘I work quite hard and earn enough to live on, so—yes, I'm doing well.’

‘I've thought about you often,’ Estella said.

‘Have you?’

‘Very often lately. For a long, difficult time I kept myself from remembering what I'd thrown away without understanding its value. But since allowing myself that memory no longer conflicted with my duty, I've made room for it in my heart.’

‘You've always had your place in my heart,’ I replied.

We fell silent again until she spoke.

‘I never imagined,’ Estella said, ‘that saying goodbye to this place would mean saying goodbye to you as well. I'm very glad to have the chance.’

‘Glad to part again, Estella? Parting hurts me. Remembering our last goodbye has always brought me sorrow and pain.’

‘But you said to me,’ Estella answered with deep earnestness, ‘“God bless you, God forgive you!” If you could say that then, you won't hesitate to say it now—now that suffering has taught me more powerfully than anything else, and has made me understand what your heart was like. I've been bent and broken, but—I hope—reshaped into something better.’

Poor Jack was later shot by Lord Canterville in a duel on Wandsworth Common, and Lady Barbara died of a broken heart at Tunbridge Wells before the year ended. So, by every measure, it had been a great success. The costume was extremely difficult to put together, however—if I may borrow theatrical language to describe one of the greatest mysteries of the supernatural, or, more scientifically, the higher-natural world. His preparations took a full three hours. At last he was ready, and he was delighted with his appearance. The outfit's large leather riding boots were a little too big, and he had found only one of the two horse pistols, but overall he was thoroughly satisfied. At one fifteen he slipped out through the wooden panelling and crept along the corridor. He reached the twins' room, which, I should add, was known as the Blue Bed Chamber because of the colour of its curtains and hangings. Its door stood slightly open. Hoping to make a dramatic entrance, he threw it wide, and a heavy jug of water came down straight onto him. It drenched him completely and missed his left shoulder by only a couple of inches. At the same instant, muffled shrieks of laughter rose from the four-poster bed. His nerves were so badly shaken that he raced back to his room as fast as possible, and the following day he was confined there with a terrible cold. His only consolation was that he had left his head behind. Had he brought it, the consequences might have been very serious.

He now abandoned any hope of frightening this ill-mannered American family. For the most part, he settled for creeping through the corridors in soft cloth slippers, with a thick red scarf wrapped around his throat to protect him from draughts. He also carried a small arquebus in case the twins attacked him. The final blow came on September 19. He had gone down to the great entrance hall, convinced that there, at least, nobody would bother him. He was entertaining himself by making sarcastic comments about the large Saroni photographs of the American Minister and his wife that had replaced the Canterville family portraits. His dress was simple but tidy: a long burial shroud marked with graveyard mould. He had bound his jaw with a strip of yellow linen and carried a small lantern and a sexton's spade.

On one occasion, however, the lieutenant inquired why he had ventured so far over the ice in such an unusual conveyance.

His face at once darkened with the profoundest sorrow, and he answered, ‘To find someone who escaped from me.’

‘Was the man you followed travelling in the same manner?’

‘He was.’

‘Then I believe we may have seen him. The day before we took you aboard, we noticed dogs pulling a sledge over the ice, with a man riding in it.’

The stranger's interest was immediately awakened, and he put innumerable questions about the direction taken by the dæmon, as he termed him. A little later, when we were alone, he said to me, ‘I have surely stirred your curiosity, and that of these kind people too; but your consideration prevents you from questioning me.’

‘Indeed; to burden you with my curiosity would be both intrusive and unfeeling.’

‘Yet you saved me from a situation as extraordinary as it was dangerous; through your kindness you have brought me back to life.’

Shortly afterward he asked whether I believed the breaking ice had destroyed the second sledge. I told him I could say nothing with certainty. The ice had remained intact until almost midnight, and the traveller might have reached safety beforehand, though I had no means of judging whether he had.

From that moment, a fresh vitality seemed to stir within the stranger's wasted body. He showed the keenest desire to go on deck and look out for the sledge we had previously observed. I have nevertheless prevailed upon him to stay in the cabin, since he is much too feeble to endure the biting air. I have assured him that someone will keep watch in his place and inform him immediately should anything new come into view.

This brings my account of that singular occurrence up to the present. The stranger's health has improved little by little, but he speaks seldom and seems troubled whenever anyone other than myself comes into his cabin. His manner, however, is so gentle and engaging that all the sailors take an interest in him, despite having exchanged very few words with him. As for me, I am beginning to feel a brother's love for him. His unceasing, profound sorrow moves me to pity and sympathy. He must have been a noble being in happier days, for even in his ruined condition he remains so amiable and appealing.

In one of my letters, dear Margaret, I told you I should find no friend upon the great ocean. Yet here I have discovered a man whom, before suffering broke his spirit, I would gladly have welcomed as the brother of my heart.
